title: Signal and Static Anew
premise: Kestrel Oyelaran, caretaker of Earth's abandoned seed vault, has spent three years hauling cargo through contested orbits under a false registry, hiding from the Consortium that once employed them. When the manifest of the Meridian—a ship that never flew—lists Kestrel's real name, they realize someone is broadcasting their identity across dead space, forcing them out of hiding. Racing to reach the edge-of-dead-space relay before the jump window closes, Kestrel teams up with Ilsa Vane, a Consortium defector whose love complicates every choice between duty and escape. At the relay, Kestrel discovers the signal was sent by their former mentor, who wants them to inherit control of the vault's genetic archive—and the power it represents. Kestrel chooses to broadcast the archive freely to all colonies, destroying their own claim to it, and leaves with Ilsa as the jump window closes.
about_author: W. M. Dunmore is the pen name of a former logistics analyst who spent a decade writing technical manuals for orbital freight companies before turning to fiction. They live in a coastal town where they still track shipping lanes for pleasure and insist that cargo manifests are the most underrated narrative form in existence.

chapters.title: The Weight of Empty Shelves
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A routine supply run to the abandoned Svalbard-style seed vault establishes Kestrel's solitary life tending Earth's genetic legacy while hauling quiet cargo through contested orbits. The emotional beat is comfortable loneliness—the ache of chosen isolation that Kestrel mistakes for peace.

chapters.title: A Ship That Never Flew
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Docking at Ceres station, Kestrel finds the Meridian—an unregistered hull with no flight history—on the schedule, its manifest bearing Kestrel's true name, unused for three years. Panic sets in: someone knows. The beat is dread breaking through routine, the past arriving like weather.

chapters.title: Ilsa Vane Boards
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. A Consortium defector forces her way aboard Kestrel's hauler claiming she can trace the manifest leak. Distrust crackles between them, but her knowledge of Consortium routing saves them from a customs trap. The beat is wary attraction—two people recognizing each other's masks.

chapters.title: Contested Orbit
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Pirates working Consortium contracts board the hauler hunting the Meridian's manifest. Kestrel jettisons legitimate cargo to escape, burning money and cover in one move. Ilsa proves herself under fire. The beat is the cost of being seen—visibility as vulnerability.

chapters.title: What the Vault Remembers
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. In the long transit, Ilsa confesses she helped design the identity-broadcast system now hunting Kestrel, and that she defected when it was turned on civilians. Kestrel cannot forgive, but cannot leave her either. The beat is intimacy built on shared guilt rather than trust.

chapters.title: Dead Space Radio
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Approaching the relay, they intercept fragments of the signal: an old voice reciting vault access codes only one person alive should know—Dr. Amara Osei, Kestrel's mentor, presumed dead. Hope and terror arrive together. The beat is grief reopening like a wound.

chapters.title: The Jump Window
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Consortium warships converge on the relay; the jump window shrinks to hours. Ilsa offers Kestrel a clean escape route that means abandoning the signal forever. Kestrel refuses. The beat is love against duty—Ilsa choosing to stay despite believing Kestrel is choosing death.

chapters.title: Amara
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Inside the relay, Kestrel finds Amara alive but dying, sustained by the station's failing systems. She reveals the truth: she faked her death to protect the archive from Consortium seizure, and broadcast Kestrel's name deliberately—to make them inherit it. The beat is betrayal braided with devotion.

chapters.title: Signal and Static
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Amara dies as Consortium marines breach the relay. Kestrel, holding the archive's master key, faces the corruption of power: the codes could grant them dominion over humanity's food future. Instead, Kestrel opens the archive to every colony, broadcasting it wide. The beat is climax—power refused at the moment of possession.

chapters.title: After the Broadcast
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Ilsa's shared POV. With the window closing, they jump through together as the archive spreads beyond anyone's control, including theirs. The vault stands empty again, but this time by design. The beat is resolution—belonging found not in a place or a legacy, but in a person, moving forward.
